title: Diognetus's questions
sum: The writer greets 'most excellent Diognetus', a man eager to learn about the Christians, and lists his questions: what God they trust and how they worship him, that they think nothing of death; why they reject the Greek gods and do not keep the Jewish observances; what their love for one another is; and why this 'new race' has appeared only now. He prays that he may speak and Diognetus hear in a way that will make Diognetus better.
The rest of the letter (2-10) answers these questions, though not one by one. Chapters 11-12, which follow in the one manuscript, are another work (see chapter 11).

views.H: Lake: Diognetus 'is unknown', and the work may be 'an academic treatise or possibly the exercise of some young theologian rather than an actual apology sent to a living person'. Some scholars have linked him to a teacher of Marcus Aurelius; the Catholic Encyclopedia calls that 'at most plausible'.
views.N: The courtesy title 'most excellent' is the one Luke gives Theophilus (Luke 1:3). Like Luke, the writer addresses one inquirer by name.
views.A: The opening states an apologist's agenda: why Christians reject both Greek religion and Judaism, why they do not fear death, and why the faith is new. These were the charges and puzzles outsiders raised.

echoes: Luke 1:3; Acts 17:22; Acts 25:19; Romans 12:10; 1 Peter 3:15; Martyrdom of Polycarp 3:2

settings.what: The letter to Diognetus: a defense of the Christian faith in answer to an inquirer's questions
settings.by: An unknown Christian writer; the one manuscript credited it to Justin Martyr, which Lake rules out
settings.to: 'Most excellent Diognetus' (1:1), a man of rank who had asked careful questions about the Christians; who he was is unknown
settings.when: Uncertain. Lake: probably later than the other Apostolic Fathers; Harnack thought the third century more likely than the second; 'there is nothing in the internal evidence to justify any certainty of opinion'.
settings.why: To answer Diognetus's questions and win him: to show that idols are nothing (2), that the Jewish sacrifices and observances are not the right worship (3-4), that Christians are model citizens whose home is heaven (5-6), that God himself sent his Word (7-8), why he sent him so late (9), and what faith would do for Diognetus himself (10). Knowing that it speaks to an educated pagan explains why it never quotes Scripture by formula and never names Jesus: it argues from reason, from the Christians' lives and from what God has done.
settings.readers: No one is known to have read it in the early church: Lake says 'early tradition does not mention the epistle'. It survived in a single manuscript of the 1200s or 1300s, once owned by Reuchlin and burned at Strasburg in 1870. Its first known readers are the scholars who copied and printed it from about 1580 on.
views: An apology sent to a real inquirer of rank, as its address says.
Lake: its style is 'rhetorical in the extreme' and it may be 'an academic treatise or possibly the exercise of some young theologian rather than an actual apology sent to a living person'.

title: Gods of stone and metal
sum: Diognetus must clear his mind and look at the gods he worships: stone like paving, bronze like pots, rotting wood, silver that needs guarding, rusting iron, clay. A craftsman could have made the same material into kitchenware. They are mute, blind and without feeling. The worshipers themselves insult them by guarding the precious ones and leaving the cheap ones out, and the 'honors' of blood and smoke would be punishment to anything that could feel.
The argument is the Hebrew prophets' (Isaiah 44; Jeremiah 10; Psalm 115), told with Greek wit.
readings: Read with the prophets
The writer follows Isaiah 44:9-20, Jeremiah 10:3-5 and Psalm 115:4-8 closely in thought: the idol is the work of human hands, without senses, and those who make it become like it.
Read as Greek rhetoric
The rapid questions, the mockery and the joke about the paving stone are the style of a trained speaker. Lake calls the style 'rhetorical in the extreme'.

views.H: Lake's one note on this chapter (2:3) explains the hard grammar: any ordinary material 'might at any moment be turned into a ‘god.’'
views.N: The New Testament's own verdict on idols is behind the chapter: 'an idol is' nothing (1 Corinthians 10:19), and the Gentiles 'traded the glory of the immortal God for a likeness' (Romans 1:23).
views.A: The writer names no Greek authority: he argues from the materials themselves. Justin makes the same case (First Apology 9: idols are 'soulless and dead').

echoes: Isaiah 44:9-20; Jeremiah 10:3-5; Psalm 115:4-8; Psalm 135:15-18; Habakkuk 2:18-19; Wisdom of Solomon 13:10; Romans 1:22-23

title: The God who needs nothing
sum: Next, why Christians do not worship as the Jews do. The Jews are right to worship one God, the Master of all, and to keep away from idols. But they offer him sacrifices as if he needed them. The one who made heaven and earth and supplies everything needs nothing. Those who honor him with blood, fat and burnt offerings are, the writer says, no different from those who make offerings to deaf idols.

views.H: Lake: like most early apologies, the work moves from 'the foolishness of the worship of idols' to 'the inadequacy of the Jewish religion'.
views.N: Lake's margin at 3:4 gives Exodus 20:11, Psalm 146:6 and Acts 14:15. Psalm 50 and Acts 17:24-25 make the point that God needs nothing; neither says that sacrifice itself was folly.
views.A: Justin: 'God does not need the material offerings which men can give' (First Apology 10).

deep.b: The writer never says that God commanded the sacrifices, which the Law says on every page (Leviticus 1:1-2). Hebrews takes a different road: the sacrifices were God's own 'shadow of the good things to come' (Hebrews 10:1), fulfilled in Christ. The Epistle of Barnabas, on this site, argues from the prophets that God 'needs no sacrifices' and 'did away with these things' (Epistle of Barnabas 2:4-6). Diognetus simply sets them beside idol worship. The canon note at 3:5 weighs this against the Bible.

echoes: Exodus 20:11; Psalm 146:6; Acts 14:15; Acts 17:24-25; Psalm 50:9-13; Hebrews 10:1-4; Isaiah 1:11

title: Foods, Sabbaths and new moons
sum: The writer dismisses the rest of Jewish practice as not worth a word: the food laws, the Sabbath, circumcision, fasts and new moons. To accept some foods and refuse others is 'lawless'; to say God forbids doing good on the Sabbath is to slander him; to boast of circumcision as proof of being chosen deserves mockery; to fix feasts and mourning by the moon is folly. Christians are right to keep away from all this. But the mystery of their own faith cannot be learned from a human being.
readings: Read as the writer meant it
An outsider's case for why Christians, though they worship Israel's God, do not keep Israel's law: the practices are human fussiness, and the true worship is a mystery revealed by God (4:6).
Read beside the Bible

The Law presents every one of these practices as God's command to Israel, and the New Testament, while freeing Gentile believers from them, never mocks them. The note at 4:1 sets out how the chapter is read today.

views.H: The chapter shows how a Christian writer, probably of the second or third century (Lake's dates), could speak of Judaism to a pagan: with mockery.
views.N: The New Testament frees Gentiles from the food laws, Sabbath and feasts (Mark 7:19; Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16; Acts 15:10), but Paul counts 'the covenants, and the lawgiving, and the sacred service' among Israel's gifts (Romans 9:4).
views.A: The words the writer chooses (jumpy fear, superstition, bragging, pretense, fussing) make the observances look foolish to a Greek reader.

echoes: Mark 3:4; Mark 7:19; Matthew 12:12; Romans 2:28-29; Romans 9:4; Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16; Philippians 3:2; 1 Timothy 4:3-4

title: Citizens and strangers
sum: The most quoted passage of the letter. Christians have no country, language or customs of their own; they live in Greek and foreign cities and follow local ways. Yet their citizenship is a paradox: at home in their own lands but as resident aliens, citizens in everything and strangers in everything. They marry and have children but do not abandon their babies; they share their table but not their beds. They are in the flesh but do not live by it; they live on earth as citizens of heaven; they obey the laws and outdo them.

Then a chain of contrasts drawn from Paul (2 Corinthians 6:9-10): loving all and persecuted by all, unknown and condemned, killed and made alive, poor and making many rich, insulted and blessing. Jews fight them and Greeks persecute them, and no one can say why.
readings: Read as a picture of Christian life
A description of how Christians live in society: fully part of it, never at home in it. The Catholic Catechism quotes 5:5 and 5:10 on the duties of citizens (2240).
Read as apology
An answer to the charge that Christians were disloyal or immoral: they keep the laws, care for their children, guard their marriages, and do good even to those who harm them.

views.H: The passage is an idealized portrait, offered to an outsider. It tells what the writer wanted Diognetus to see, and what Christians aimed at.
views.N: Lake's margin marks the sources: 2 Corinthians 10:3 and Romans 8:12-13 (5:8), Philippians 3:18-20 (5:9), 2 Corinthians 6:9-10 (5:11-16), 1 Corinthians 4:12 (5:15). 1 Peter's 'resident aliens' (1 Peter 2:11) and Hebrews' 'country in heaven' (Hebrews 11:16) stand behind 5:5.
views.A: The language is the Greek city's: politeia, citizens, homelands, laws. The writer presents Christians as better citizens than the city's own, which was the apologists' standard answer to the charge of disloyalty.

deep.b: A paroikos lived in a city with a place but without a citizen's rights. The Greek Old Testament uses the word for Abraham (Genesis 23:4) and for Israel before God (Leviticus 25:23; Psalm 39:12, which is Psalm 38:13 in the Greek numbering); 1 Peter makes it the name of Christians (1 Peter 1:17; 1 Peter 2:11), and early Christian letters open with a church 'that lives as a resident alien' in Rome, Corinth, Philippi or Smyrna (1 Clement 1:0; Polycarp to the Philippians 1:0; Martyrdom of Polycarp 1:0). Diognetus 5 works the idea out at length. The topic page Strangers and Exiles follows it through the Bible.

The chapter raises the question how far Christians must obey the state and when they may refuse. The site asks it at Romans 13 ('Must Christians always obey the government, and when may they resist?') and Matthew 22, with each church's answer; this chapter adds no card of its own.

echoes: 1 Peter 1:17; 1 Peter 2:11; Hebrews 11:13-16; Philippians 3:20; 2 Corinthians 10:3; Romans 8:12-13; 2 Corinthians 6:9-10; 1 Corinthians 4:12; Ephesians 2:19; Jeremiah 29:7

title: The soul of the world
sum: One image in ten verses: what the soul is to the body, Christians are in the world. The soul is spread through the body, as Christians through the cities; it lives in the body but is not from it; it is invisible, as their faith is; the flesh hates it, as the world hates them, though neither has been wronged; it loves the body that hates it; it is shut in the body yet holds it together, as Christians hold the world together; it is immortal in a mortal tent; it grows better under hardship, as Christians grow under punishment. God has stationed them at this post, and they may not refuse it.

views.H: Lake compares 6:7 with Aristides, Apology 16: the world 'stands through the intercession of Christians'. He takes 6:10 as the idea of the church as God's army.
views.N: Lake's margin: John 17:11-16 (6:3), Galatians 5:17 (6:4-5), John 15:18-19 (6:5), Matthew 5:44 and Luke 6:27 (6:6).
views.A: The picture of the soul imprisoned in the body is Greek; the writer uses it to say something the Bible says in other words: that God's people are 'the salt of the earth' (Matthew 5:13). The canon note at 6:5 weighs the difference.

deep.title: Claude's theory: why the soul, and not the city
deep.b: This is Claude's own reading. Chapter 5 described Christians as citizens of heaven living as resident aliens; chapter 6 switches to the soul in the body. The switch answers an objection a Roman would raise to chapter 5: if Christians are only foreigners here, what good are they to the city? The soul is a 'foreigner' in the body (6:3) and yet the body's life (6:7). The writer thus turns the charge of disloyalty around: the city's life depends on the strangers in it. The likeness to Aristides that Lake notes (6:7) shows the thought was at hand; the link between the two chapters is Claude's observation.

echoes: John 17:11-16; John 15:18-19; Galatians 5:17; Matthew 5:13-14; Matthew 5:44; 1 Peter 2:11; 2 Corinthians 5:1-4

title: God sent his Word
sum: The Christians' faith is not a human discovery. God himself, Almighty and invisible, set the truth and his holy Word among people. He did not send an angel or a ruler, but the Craftsman and Creator of everything, whom the sun, moon, stars and elements obey. He sent him not as a tyrant but in gentleness, 'as a king sends his son', as God and as a human being, to save and persuade, 'for force has no place in God'. He will send him again as judge, and who will stand?

Here the manuscript has a gap. It resumes with the martyrs: thrown to wild beasts to make them deny the Lord, they are not overcome, and the more are punished, the more others join. These are God's power and proofs of his coming.

views.H: Lake marks a gap after 7:6 and suggests the next sentence began 'Do you not see that'. How much is lost cannot be known.
views.N: Lake's margin: 1 Corinthians 9:17 (7:1), Zechariah 9:9 (7:3), John 3:17 (7:4-5), Malachi 3:2 (7:6). The Word as agent of creation is John 1:3, Colossians 1:16 and Hebrews 1:2.
views.A: The writer never names Jesus. He speaks of the Logos, a word that to a Greek reader also meant the reason that orders the world, and he describes him as the Craftsman (technitēs) and Creator (dēmiourgos), words a philosopher would know.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the moon watched and the moon obeying
deep.b: This is Claude's own observation, not a published reading as far as the sources opened here show. At 4:5 the writer mocks Jews who 'keep close watch on the stars and the moon' to fix their feasts. At 7:2 the same moon and stars appear again, now obeying the Word who commands them. The two passages seem built as a pair: the heavens are not a calendar for human religion to read, but servants of the one God sent. If so, the writer's answer to Jewish practice is not only mockery but a claim: the one who rules the moon has come.

echoes: John 1:1-3; Colossians 1:15-17; Hebrews 1:2; Zechariah 9:9; John 3:17; Malachi 3:2; Job 38:8-11; Psalm 104:19; Wisdom of Solomon 13:1

title: No one knew God until he came
sum: Before he came, no one knew what God is. The philosophers called God fire or water or some other element God made, which would make any created thing a god: it is the trickery of sorcerers. No one has seen God; he has shown himself, through faith. He has always been kind, good, free from anger and true. He conceived a great thought and shared it with his Child alone; while he kept it hidden he seemed not to care, but when he revealed it through his beloved Child he gave us everything at once.

views.H: The attack on the philosophers puts the work among the apologists, as Lake says it belongs by its contents.
views.N: John 1:18 ('Nobody has ever seen God') and 1 Timothy 6:16 stand behind 8:5. The hidden and revealed plan is Paul's 'mystery' (Romans 16:25; Colossians 1:26).
views.A: The writer is harder on the philosophers than Justin, who held that 'those who lived reasonably are Christians' (First Apology 46). See the canon note at 8:1 and the topic Knowing God from Creation.

echoes: John 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:16; Hebrews 11:6; Romans 1:19-20; Acts 17:22-31; Wisdom of Solomon 13:1-2; Romans 16:25; Colossians 1:26; 1 Corinthians 2:9

title: Why the Son came so late
sum: God had planned everything with his Child from the start, but he let humanity follow its desires, not because he liked our sins but to let us prove we could not reach life on our own. When our wrongdoing was complete and its wages, punishment and death, were waiting, God did not hate us. He bore with us, took up our sins, and handed over his own Son as a ransom: the holy for the lawless, the righteous for the unrighteous, the immortal for the mortal. 'Oh, the sweet exchange!' The lawlessness of many is hidden in one righteous man, and the righteousness of one justifies many. So God wants us to trust his kindness and to see him as father, teacher, doctor, light and life.
readings: Read as an answer to 'why now?'
The chapter answers Diognetus's last question (1:1): God waited so that human beings would learn their own inability and receive life as a gift.
Read as teaching on the cross
The letter's fullest passage on Christ's death: ransom, substitution ('the holy for the lawless'), covering of sins, justification and exchange. The views note at 9:5 says how readers take it.

views.H: The passage cannot be dated by its theology with any certainty; Lake finds 'nothing in the internal evidence to justify any certainty'.
views.N: Lake's margin: Romans 3:21-26, Titus 3:3-5, John 3:5 (9:1); Romans 8:32, Ephesians 1:7, 1 Timothy 2:6, 1 Peter 3:18 (9:2); Matthew 6:25-31 (9:6). The 'exchange' of 9:5 sits beside 2 Corinthians 5:21 and Romans 5:18-19.
views.A: Against the pagan charge that a new religion cannot be true, the writer offers a history of God's patience. He never names Jesus; the Son, the servant and the Savior carry the argument.

deep.b: How the cross saves is asked on the site at 2 Corinthians 5 ('How does the cross save?'), Romans 3 ('How does Christ's death save?'), Galatians 3 and 1 John 2, with each church's answer and its sources. This chapter is often read alongside those passages, but it adds no card: its own words are given in the notes.

echoes: Romans 3:21-26; Romans 5:6-10; Romans 5:18-19; Romans 6:23; Romans 8:32; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Titus 3:3-5; 1 Peter 3:18; 1 Timothy 2:6; Mark 10:45; Isaiah 53:11; Galatians 4:4

title: Imitators of God
sum: If Diognetus wants this faith, he will first receive knowledge of the Father, and here the manuscript has a gap. It resumes with God's love for humankind: he made the world for us, gave us reason and mind, formed us from his image, sent his only Son, and promised his kingdom. Knowing him, how could one not love him? And loving him, one becomes an imitator of his kindness: not by domination or wealth, but by carrying a neighbor's burden and giving to the needy what one has from God, so becoming 'a god to those who receive it'.

Then Diognetus will see that God's city is in heaven, will admire the martyrs who will not deny God, and will fear the real death of the eternal fire more than the short fire of execution. Here, as it survives, the letter ends.

views.H: Lake marks a second gap after 10:1, though Otto (1879) read the sentence as complete (see the variant). The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the letter 'breaks off at the end of chapter x; it may have originally been much longer'.
views.N: Lake's margin: John 3:16 and 1 John 4:9 (10:1-2), Genesis 1:26-27 (10:2), 1 John 4:19 (10:3), Galatians 6:2 (10:5-6), Ephesians 6:9 and Colossians 4:1 (10:6).
views.A: The chapter offers the inquirer what a philosopher's school offered: happiness (10:5), but defined as imitating God's generosity, not as self-mastery or power.

echoes: John 3:16; 1 John 4:9-10; 1 John 4:19; Genesis 1:26-27; Ephesians 5:1; Luke 6:36; Galatians 6:2; Matthew 25:41; Matthew 10:28; Martyrdom of Polycarp 11:2

title: A different voice: the Word from the beginning
sum: Here begins a separate work. Lake: chapters 11-12 'have clearly no connection with the preceding ones', and 'it is generally conceded that they belong to a different document, probably an Epiphany homily, though possibly, as Otto thought, an Easter homily'; Bonwetsch argued 'very strong reasons' for Hippolytus as the author. The site keeps Lake's numbers, which run on from the letter.

The preacher calls himself 'a disciple of apostles' and 'a teacher of the nations'. He speaks of the Word who appeared, taught the disciples the Father's mysteries, was dishonored by 'the people' and believed by the nations; who was from the beginning, appeared new, and is born young in the saints' hearts; who 'today' is reckoned as Son. Through him grace is multiplied, the Law and Prophets, the Gospels and the apostles' tradition are honored, and the church rejoices.
readings: Read as a sermon for a feast
The 'today' of 11:5 and the 'Lord's Passover' of 12:9 suggest a homily for a feast day: the Nativity and Epiphany, Lake thought, or Easter, as Otto did.
Read as an ending to the letter

Before modern scholars separated the chapters, readers took them as the letter's close, and the phrase 'disciple of apostles' made the whole work look very early. The Catholic Encyclopedia says it was 'through a misunderstanding of these words' that the epistle has 'since the eighteenth century' been classed among the Apostolic Fathers.

views.H: A different document, by Lake's judgment and the Catholic Encyclopedia's; probably a homily; possibly by Hippolytus (Bonwetsch, 1902, as Lake reports). The style changes from the letter's clear argument to the 'florid and obscure' (Catholic Encyclopedia).
views.N: Lake's margin: John 1:9 (11:2), 1 Timothy 3:16 and 1 John 1:1 (11:3-4), Psalm 2:7 and Matthew 3:17 (11:5). The homily's Word is John's.
views.A: Unlike the letter, the homily speaks to believers ('those who are becoming disciples of the truth'), not to an outsider.

echoes: John 1:1-14; 1 John 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:16; Psalm 2:7; Matthew 3:17; Proverbs 22:28; Ephesians 4:30; 1 Timothy 2:7

settings.what: A homily (sermon) on the Word and on the two trees of paradise, joined to the letter in the one manuscript
settings.by: An unknown preacher who calls himself 'a disciple of apostles' and 'a teacher of the nations' (11:1); Bonwetsch argued for Hippolytus of Rome, as Lake reports
settings.to: Christian hearers, 'those who are becoming disciples of the truth' (11:1), addressed as 'you' (11:7; 12:1, 7)
settings.when: At a feast: Lake reads the 'today' of 11:5 as pointing to the Nativity, 'in the time of Hippolytus ... probably not separated from the Epiphany or feast of the Baptism'; Otto took it for an Easter homily (12:9, 'the Lord's Passover'). Otto (1879) held that it was written in the third century or a little later.
settings.why: To lead believers who already have the faith deeper into it: to know the Word who was from the beginning, to keep the tradition of the apostles, and to join knowledge with life, as the two trees of paradise stood together (12:1-8). Knowing that it is a sermon to the church, not part of the letter to Diognetus, keeps the reader from taking 'disciple of apostles' as a claim by the letter's writer to have known the apostles.
settings.readers: Lake: 'probably an Epiphany homily', so a congregation at a feast; who they were and where is not known. The piece survived only because a copyist placed it after the letter in the manuscript burned in 1870.
views: Otto, as Lake reports; 12:9 speaks of 'the Lord's Passover'.

title: The two trees of paradise
sum: Those who love God rightly become 'a paradise of delight', with a fruitful tree growing in them. In the garden God planted a tree of knowledge and a tree of life together: knowledge does not kill; disobedience kills. There is no life without knowledge and no safe knowledge without true life. That is why Paul warns that 'knowledge puffs up, but love builds up'. Whoever knows with fear and seeks life plants in hope. Let your heart be knowledge and your life the true word: then the snake cannot touch you, Eve is not corrupted, a virgin is trusted, salvation is shown, the Lord's Passover goes forward, and the Word, through whom the Father is glorified, rejoices. To him be glory forever.
readings: Read as a reading of Genesis
The homily reads Genesis 2-3 as a picture of the soul: the two trees belong together, and the fall came from using knowledge 'not purely'. The canon note at 12:2 weighs this against Genesis.
Read against false knowledge
The stress on knowledge joined to life and love, with Paul's 'knowledge puffs up', may answer teachers who prized knowledge apart from obedience. The homily names no opponents.

views.H: The last verses, with 'the Lord's Passover' and 'the seasons brought together', fit a homily for a feast (see chapter 11).
views.N: Lake's margin: Genesis 2:15 and 3:24 (12:1), Genesis 2:9 (12:2), 1 Corinthians 8:1 (12:5, the only quotation by formula in the work), 1 Corinthians 9:10 (12:6).
views.A: The homily has left the apologetic world of the letter behind; it speaks the church's language of Eve, the virgin, the apostles and Pascha.

echoes: Genesis 2:8-17; Genesis 3:1-24; 1 Corinthians 8:1-2; 1 Corinthians 9:10; 2 Corinthians 11:2-3; Luke 1:38; Revelation 2:7; Revelation 22:2
